name: Aquaphor

lead: Aquaphor is an over-the-counter ointment from Beiersdorf whose active ingredient is petrolatum (41%), with mineral oil, ceresin, lanolin alcohol, glycerin, panthenol and bisabolol [1]. It is used to protect minor cuts and scrapes and to treat chapped or cracked skin [1].

Its appearance use is skin and lip repair: it keeps skin moist and protected, which is why surgeons and dermatologists use it after procedures such as laser resurfacing, where smoother healing matters for the look of the skin [2][3][4].

paras: It is applied in a thin layer to dry lips, chapped patches, healing wounds or post-procedure skin, and clinicians recommend it for minor post-operative wounds [1]. Forum users also discuss it as a barrier on the eye area, for example alongside topical minoxidil or Latisse, and as a lip product during isotretinoin courses [5][6].

The ointment is free of fragrances, dyes and preservatives and is described as non-comedogenic, but contains wool-derived lanolin alcohol [1]. A case report asked whether bisabolol was the culprit in reactions to it [7]. Heavy occlusive ointments can be messy and stain clothing, as T Nation posters note [6].

angle.text: Used on dry lips and skin and on freshly treated skin after lasers and surgery to keep it moist while it heals.

lead: Aquaphor is an over-the-counter healing ointment made by Beiersdorf, a German skin-care company. Its active ingredient is 41% petrolatum, listed under the US skin-protectant monograph, and it is labelled to protect minor cuts, scrapes and burns and chapped or cracked skin [1]. It sits beside Eucerin and Nivea in the Beiersdorf portfolio and descends from the lanolin-alcohol ointment bases the company developed in the early 1900s [1][2][3].

For appearance, the product is used as a barrier on dry lips, chapped patches and skin that is healing after cosmetic procedures. The chain is simple: a petrolatum-based film slows moisture loss from the skin surface, which keeps the area supple while it heals, and smoother-looking skin and lips follow [1][4]. Dermatologic surgeons have used it as the post-procedure dressing after facial laser resurfacing, and it often serves as the standard-of-care comparator in trials of newer post-procedure products [5][6][7][8].

In looksmaxxing and lifting communities it turns up in three places: on the eye area alongside bimatoprost (Latisse) or topical minoxidil, as a lip and skin product during isotretinoin courses, and as tattoo aftercare [9][10][11][12]. Reviews of post-surgical wound care have examined petrolatum and multi-ingredient ointments such as Aquaphor against each other, and Wikipedia notes that no studies have tested this brand's own healing claims [1][13].
infobox: Mineral oil, ceresin, lanolin alcohol, glycerin, panthenol, bisabolol [1]
Healing Ointment, Lip Repair, Baby, Advanced Therapy [1]

paras: Aquaphor Healing Ointment is an anhydrous (water-free) ointment. Wikipedia lists its active ingredient as 41% petrolatum, per the FDA's over-the-counter skin-protectant monograph, with mineral oil, ceresin (a purified wax), lanolin alcohol, glycerin, panthenol (pro-vitamin B5) and bisabolol (a chamomile-derived compound) as other components. The maker describes it as free of fragrance, dyes and preservatives and as non-comedogenic [1].

Unlike Vaseline, which is 100% petrolatum, Aquaphor is marketed as a semi-occlusive barrier that is described as letting some water and oxygen pass; Wikipedia adds that no studies have tested the brand's specific healing claims [1]. Because lanolin alcohol comes from sheep wool, the product is not vegan or vegetarian, and Wikipedia notes the glycerin in US products is mostly animal-derived [1].

The label indication is temporary protection of minor cuts, scrapes and burns and of chapped or cracked skin, and healthcare professionals use and recommend it for minor post-operative wounds [1]. The product line has grown to include a lip repair range, baby products and larger tubs for body use [1].

Aquaphor's lineage runs through Beiersdorf's early skin-care chemistry. The company was founded in Hamburg in 1882 by the pharmacist Paul Beiersdorf; Oscar Troplowitz bought it in 1890 and later worked with the dermatologist Paul Gerson Unna and the chemist Isaac Lifschütz [3]. Lifschütz produced an ointment base from the emulsifier Eucerit, water and oil around 1900 and patented his method in Germany in 1902; Troplowitz bought the patent in 1911 [2]. Nivea Creme, launched in December 1911, used the same emulsifier [3].

According to Wikipedia, the ointment was developed in Beiersdorf's US laboratories and the Aquaphor trademark was registered in 1925 by company president Herman A. Metz [1]. Beiersdorf sold the trademarks to Duke Laboratories in 1929; the first product was sold in 1936 in 5-pound containers to doctors, pharmacists and hospitals. Production stopped during World War II and resumed in 1960 in 1-pound cans and 2-ounce tubes for medical professionals [1]. (Grokipedia gives a 1924 trademark date and a 1936 first launch; the Wikipedia dates are used here where they differ [14].)

Beiersdorf bought the trademarks back in 1973 and sold Aquaphor directly to consumers for the first time in 1982 [1]. Advanced Therapy Healing Ointment followed in 1991, baby products in 2003 and a lip repair line in 2011; in 2012 the brand launched in 25 further countries, and in 2013 it earned the Good Housekeeping Seal [1]. Grokipedia also describes a 2022 'Before and Aquaphor' campaign and says dermatologists have ranked the brand as a leading recommendation for dry, cracked skin; these points come from an AI-generated page and are not independently confirmed here [14].

Petrolatum is the best-known occlusive in skin care. Wikipedia's article on petroleum jelly says that by reducing transepidermal water loss it can help prevent chapped hands and lips and soften cuticles, and that the American Academy of Dermatology recommends keeping skin injuries moist to reduce scarring [4]. The same article notes that petrolatum was long regarded purely as an occlusive, while newer claims that it penetrates the stratum corneum and improves absorption of other products are not well sourced [4].

Aquaphor adds a mix of emollient, wax and humectant ingredients to that petrolatum base. The manufacturer frames the glycerin and panthenol as moisturising components and bisabolol as an anti-inflammatory chamomile derivative [1]. Laser surgeons who favour open dressings use it to reduce moisture loss from treated skin [6].

The most common everyday use is as a lip and dry-patch product. Chapped lips and flaking skin look rough, and a petrolatum-based barrier is applied to hold moisture in while the surface recovers [1]. Aquaphor sells a dedicated lip repair line, introduced in 2011, and a lip version with SPF 30 [1].

Laser surgeons who prefer open dressings have used the original Aquaphor formula to reduce moisture loss from resurfaced facial skin [6]. In dermatology trials it frequently appears as the baseline care: after radiofrequency microneedling, after non-ablative fractional laser, and after laser resurfacing, newer products are compared against Aquaphor as the standard of care [5][6][7][8].

A 2025 randomised trial of radiofrequency microneedling compared pure PDGF against Aquaphor as standard of care and reported greater improvement in the PDGF group [7]. A 2025 split-face trial compared a peptide formula with Aquaphor Healing Ointment after non-ablative laser, applying both twice daily for 28 days [8]. A further 2025 double-blind randomised study examined a niacinamide-containing formula after non-ablative laser [15]. These studies test the newer products; Aquaphor is the reference arm.

A 2026 narrative review of post-operative care after Mohs micrographic surgery examined 15 common practices. It reported at least Level III evidence for using plain petrolatum in preference to topical antibiotics and to multi-ingredient ointments such as Aquaphor, and noted that many practices vary by training tradition [13]. Mohs reconstruction is a facial procedure, so the review bears on how surgical scars and wounds on the face are managed.

Grokipedia says Aquaphor is widely recommended for tattoo aftercare, notably in Chile and elsewhere in Latin America, with the maker promoting it through Eucerin-branded ointment [14]. On T Nation, lifters discussing fresh tattoos describe it as a standard aftercare product [10][12].

sections.h: Use in looksmaxxing and lifting communities

subs.h: Eye area with bimatoprost and minoxidil
paras: A looksmax.org thread proposes using petrolatum or Aquaphor as a barrier around the eyes for people who apply bimatoprost (Latisse) for lashes or topical minoxidil for brows, with the aim of avoiding under-eye fat loss. The author quotes a study reporting smaller orbital fat volume and enophthalmos on the bimatoprost-treated side, and treats that as the mechanism the barrier is meant to address [9]. Wikipedia's bimatoprost article lists darkening of the eyelid or area beneath the eye among reported effects of the cosmetic product [16].

subs.h: Lip and skin dryness during isotretinoin
paras: Wikipedia's isotretinoin article says dry lips, skin and nose are among the most common side effects, that lip dryness occurs in almost all people taking the drug, and that regular lip balm and moisturiser are recommended throughout treatment [17]. T Nation posters describe Aquaphor in these terms: one writes that chapstick stops working and 'heavy-duty stuff' is needed, another that they carried tubes everywhere, while noting it is messy and stains [10][11][18]. Another poster ties months of moisturiser and Aquaphor to years of clearer skin afterwards [19].
Lifting forums mention it for tattoo healing and for skin around training-related wraps and dressings, usually in one-line recommendations rather than extended discussion [10][12][20].

Aquaphor is labelled for external use as a skin protectant. Its lanolin alcohol is derived from wool, which is relevant to anyone with a known lanolin allergy, and a 2010 pediatric dermatology case report asked whether bisabolol was responsible for reactions seen with the product [1][21].

Wikipedia's petroleum jelly article notes that refined petrolatum can contain mineral-oil aromatic hydrocarbons; the EU limits polycyclic aromatic hydrocarbons in cosmetics to 0.005%, EFSA issued an opinion on the topic in 2012, and pharmacopeial grades (USP, BP, Ph. Eur.) govern medical and personal-care products [4]. Users on T Nation describe heavy petrolatum ointments as messy and staining on clothing [10].

A 2002 randomised trial in 42 patients compared two wound-care regimens after full-face laser resurfacing. One arm used a dressing for the first 2 to 3 days followed by Aquaphor to complete two weeks; the other used a multi-step resurfacing recovery system [5].
A second 2002 randomised trial compared a mucopolysaccharide-cartilage complex ointment with Aquaphor, the standard therapy, for erythema, oedema and skin erosion after Er:YAG laser resurfacing [6].

In 69 premature infants born before 33 weeks, a 2010 randomised trial assigned either No-Sting skin protectant or Aquaphor for 14 days. Infants receiving Aquaphor had significantly higher Neonatal Skin Condition Scores, though both groups stayed in the normal range, and transepidermal water loss did not differ between the products [22].

The 2018 trolamine review of seven controlled trials in radiation dermatitis listed Aquaphor among the comparison treatments [23]. A 1986 study evaluated an Aquaphor gauze dressing in burned children [24].

Wikipedia also reports a 2011 manufacturer-funded study in the Journal of the American Academy of Dermatology in which the healing ointment was associated with, but not shown to cause, less redness around wounds, and which did not clinically outperform other products [1].

lore.intro: Aquaphor is discussed on looksmax.org mostly as an occlusive for the eye area and on T Nation for lips, tattoos and dry skin during isotretinoin [9][10][11][12].

timeline.event: Pharmacist Paul Beiersdorf founds the company in Hamburg [3].
Isaac Lifschütz receives a German patent for a Eucerit-based ointment base called Eucerin; Beiersdorf buys the patent in 1911 [2].
Aquaphor is introduced in the US; Herman A. Metz registers the trademark [1].
First sold in 5-pound containers to doctors, pharmacists and hospitals [1].
Production resumes after World War II in 1-pound cans and 2-ounce tubes for professionals [1].
Beiersdorf buys the trademarks back from Duke Laboratories [1].
Aquaphor Advanced Therapy Healing Ointment launches [1].
Two randomised trials use Aquaphor in post-laser facial wound care [5][6].
Lip repair line added; a manufacturer-funded JAAD study is published [1].
Randomised aesthetic trials use Aquaphor as standard of care after microneedling and laser [7][8].
